key_insight: AI can make augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) systems more capable, but evaluating those systems is not straightforward because users’ needs are highly personal, contextual, and multidimensional. The paper argues for richer evaluation methods that better reflect the real lives and goals of AAC users.
problem_solved: This paper addresses the challenge of designing and evaluating AI-powered AAC interfaces when standard metrics fail to capture the nuanced, intersectional, and individualized preferences of people who use AAC.
method: Examines six AAC problem spaces where AI could support communication.
Analyzes how AI might be applied differently across these spaces.
Proposes more robust evaluation approaches that account for complex user needs and lived experience.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this highlights that success in assistive AI cannot be measured only by accuracy or speed. It emphasizes the need for human-centered, context-aware evaluation frameworks when building tools for people with disabilities.
visual_elements: A six-part problem-space grid showing where AI can assist AAC users.
A comparison chart contrasting traditional metrics vs. user-centered AAC evaluation.
An icon-based flow showing user needs, AI support, and evaluation outcomes.
A layered diagram illustrating intersectional factors shaping AAC preferences.
paper_title: It's Complicated: On the Design and Evaluation of AI-Powered AAC Interfaces
paper_authors: Blade Frisch, Will Wade, Dylan Gaines, Michelle Kinsella, Betts Peters
